name: Financial Times cryptic crossword, Penguin book 1 No 10

book.title: The Penguin Book of Financial Times Crosswords, volume 1

clue.text: Get mother to request the fabric

blocks.note: a dam is the mother of an animal, especially a horse
to request is to ask

explanation.surface: Someone tells you to have your mother order the cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: Dam is the breeder's word for a female parent, a favourite crossword mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Damask is a reversible patterned woven cloth, often silk or linen, named after Damascus.

clue.text: Lifeless, crazy, but very keen

definitions.note: the slang phrase is used with on: very keen on something

blocks.note: lifeless means dead
nuts is slang for crazy

explanation.surface: Someone is dull and mad but full of enthusiasm all the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead nuts on' is old British slang for being extremely fond of something.
explanation.definitionFit: To be dead nuts on something is dated British slang for being enthusiastic about it, intensely fond.

clue.text: Named from a waterfall

blocks.note: surface reading: anything, a town or a drink, that takes its name from some falls
setter's reading: the heroine of Longfellow's Hiawatha, whose name means laughing water

explanation.walkthrough: In The Song of Hiawatha the hero's bride is named after a waterfall, called 'Laughing Water'; Minnehaha Falls in Minnesota shares the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Longfellow's Minnehaha takes her name from a Dakota phrase for a laughing waterfall, the cascade near her home.

clue.text: Places fought for at Wimbledon

definitions.note: places is used loosely for the units a player tries to win

blocks.note: surface reading: seats or positions people compete to get, like tickets for the tennis
setter's reading: the units of a tennis match that players battle to win

explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon is the London grass-court tennis championship; a match is won in units of six or more games.
explanation.definitionFit: A tennis match is divided into contests of games, and players at Wimbledon battle to take each one.

clue.text: Fine victories off the coast of Kent

definitions.note: a description of where the answer lies rather than a noun; the answer is the sandbanks found there

blocks.note: fine and good both mean satisfactory
victories are wins

explanation.surface: A list of excellent results reads like a sports report from somewhere on the Kent coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The Goodwins (the Goodwin Sands) are notorious shipwrecking sandbanks in the English Channel off Deal, in the county of Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: The Goodwin Sands, usually called the Goodwins, are a ten-mile sandbank lying a few miles out to sea from the Kent shore.

clue.text: bie gets round a sound attempt completely

indicators.note: a sound version of a word is one heard rather than spelt, so the next word is taken by ear
to get round something is to surround it, so one word wraps itself about the other

blocks.note: garbled in the scanned copy; the wordplay needs the word ought, meaning should, here
an attempt is a try, written here as it is pronounced

explanation.surface: Something has gone round an attempt that sounds right, and done so thoroughly.
explanation.walkthrough: The book's scan has mangled the clue's first word into 'bie', a misreading too large to mend with certainty; the crossings and the rest of the wordplay point to 'Ought'.
explanation.definitionFit: Outright means wholly or without reservation, as in an outright ban, so it can replace completely.

clue.text: You must be pretty sick to be found on it

definitions.text: You must be pretty sick to be found on it

blocks.note: surface reading: rather ill, or rather fed up, as if lying on a sickbed
setter's reading: a hospital register of patients whose condition is critical

explanation.walkthrough: 'On it' suggests lying on a bed; the thing you are on is a register of names.
explanation.definitionFit: A hospital's register of critically ill patients is the list one joins only when life is threatened.

clue.text: The girl is inside, that is stupid

indicators.note: being inside means one piece sits within another piece around it

blocks.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is
Nan is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl stays indoors, and someone judges that a foolish thing to do.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane describes something silly and lacking sense, a synonym for foolish or senseless.

clue.text: Rider gets a pass for a seat

blocks.note: first meaning: a low ridge or col between two mountain peaks
second meaning: the seat strapped on a horse, which a rider gets

explanation.walkthrough: The rider seems to be given a travel permit; 'pass' is the mountain kind, a dip between summits.
explanation.definitionFit: A saddle is a rider's seat on a horse or bicycle, and in geography a ridge between two higher points.

clue.text: The publication is to take legal proceedings

blocks.note: taken as written
to sue is to bring a lawsuit

explanation.surface: A magazine is about to be taken to court.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is one edition of a newspaper or magazine, or the act of putting something out.

clue.text: The girl has a setback with the payments

indicators.note: back joined to the word before it tells the solver to read that word in the backward direction

blocks.note: a girl's name, as so often in crosswords
taken as written
the first three letters of this word are taken as written, the rest being the turning instruction

explanation.surface: A girl suffers a financial setback over her payments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setback' looks like one word meaning a reverse, but it splits into the word and its turning instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Annates were the first year's revenue of a church benefice, paid by a new incumbent to the Pope, so they are historic payments.

clue.text: Manx legislative body

blocks.note: surface reading: a plain question asking for the parliament of the Isle of Man
setter's reading: there is no trick, the solver simply needs the island's own name for its parliament

explanation.walkthrough: This is a straight general-knowledge definition; Manx means belonging to the Isle of Man, a self-governing island in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Tynwald is the ancient parliament of the Isle of Man, claimed as the oldest continuous legislature in the world.

clue.text: Refusals put your nose out of joint

indicators.note: a dislocated limb is out of joint, so the letters here are displaced from their order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Being turned down keeps upsetting you and putting your nose out of joint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put someone's nose out of joint' is an idiom for offending them, which hides the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Noes are negative replies or votes against, so the plural fits refusals in number and sense.

clue.text: Rung twice with good news

blocks.note: surface reading: something sounded two times, like a phone or a doorbell
setter's reading: the famous bell at Lloyd's of London, struck twice to announce good news about a ship

explanation.walkthrough: The bell from HMS Lutine hangs at Lloyd's of London, the insurance market; traditionally it was rung once for a ship lost and twice for one overdue but safe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lutine Bell's ceremonial double stroke historically told underwriters that a missing vessel had arrived safely.

clue.text: No discrimination on the railway for a scoundrel

blocks.note: surface reading: a policy of equal treatment for staff or passengers on the trains
setter's reading: a railway employing a Black man as its guard, read as two words that together make the insult

explanation.walkthrough: A guard is the official in charge of a train; the dated 1970s clue splits the answer into a colour and that job.
explanation.definitionFit: A blackguard, pronounced 'blaggard', is a dishonourable man, a rogue or villain.

clue.text: Drags along the beaten paths

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, pulls behind on the ground
second meaning: a plural noun, tracks worn by walking

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures someone hauling something down well-trodden routes; the two halves are a verb and a noun spelt the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A coat that trails drags behind its wearer, and trails are rough paths made through country by use.

clue.text: Cottages Charles is about to let

indicators.note: to be about something is to be around it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: Chas is the standard written short form of the name Charles
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Charles is about to rent out his holiday homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to let' reads as a single phrase meaning ready to rent out, but 'about' is the wrapping signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalet is a small wooden house or holiday cottage, originally an Alpine herdsman's hut.

clue.text: 'I met a — from an antique land' (Shelley)

definitions.text: 'I met a — from an antique land' (Shelley)

blocks.note: surface reading: the opening line of a poem, with a word left blank
setter's reading: the missing word of the first line of Shelley's sonnet Ozymandias

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: Ozymandias opens 'I met a [answer] from an antique land, Who said...'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shelley's sonnet the speaker hears the tale of the ruined statue from a voyager who has come from Egypt.

clue.text: This kind of talk is frank and confidential

definitions.text: This kind of talk is frank and confidential

blocks.note: surface reading: a style of conversation that is open and private
setter's reading: the phrase for a candid private chat between two people on equal terms

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is almost a plain definition; the answer is a hyphenless adjectival phrase for honest one-to-one talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A man-to-man talk is a direct, honest conversation between two people, held privately and without pretence.

clue.text: A girl shut up — how wasted

blocks.note: a miss is a girl or young unmarried woman
pent means confined, as in pent-up

explanation.surface: A girl kept locked away: what a waste of a life.
explanation.definitionFit: Misspent describes time or money squandered, as in a misspent youth.

clue.text: The saint we leave for the North

definitions.note: a cryptic description of the London station, not a synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: ..., a boy martyr of Rome in the early fourth century
second meaning: St ..., the London railway terminus with trains to the Midlands and the north of England

explanation.walkthrough: St Pancras is a mainline station in London named after the saint, from which trains run north.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Pancras is a Roman martyr, and the London district and railway station named for him send travellers northwards.

clue.text: Demand change of air for the African soldier

indicators.note: a change made to something alters its arrangement, so its letters are reordered

blocks.note: to demand is to ask for
the letters of the word, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone insists the African soldier needs a change of air, as if prescribing a trip for his health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change of air' is a stock phrase for a restorative holiday, which disguises the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An askari was a local soldier or policeman serving the colonial powers in East Africa; the word is Swahili and Arabic for soldier.

clue.text: Light enters through earnest entreaty

indicators.note: something that enters goes inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: per is Latin for through, as in per annum
a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: Light shines in through an earnest plea, like sun through a church window.
explanation.definitionFit: A prayer is a solemn request, whether addressed to God or anyone else, so an earnest plea.

clue.text: Monuments — to doctors?

blocks.note: taken as written
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a British medical degree, so doctors are MBs

explanation.surface: A grim joke that memorials are built for the doctors who sent people there.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke that doctors fill graves.
explanation.definitionFit: Tombs are burial vaults or grave monuments raised over the dead.

clue.text: This is what gets a team down

definitions.text: This is what gets a team down

blocks.note: surface reading: something that depresses the players' morale
setter's reading: the process that literally moves a club down into a lower division

explanation.walkthrough: In English football leagues the bottom clubs each season drop to the division below.
explanation.definitionFit: Relegation is demotion to a lower league, which literally sends a side downwards, and certainly lowers its spirits too.

clue.text: Flying frolics

blocks.note: surface reading: quick, playful bits of fun
setter's reading: a hint that the word is also the name of a songbird that flies high, in the plural

explanation.walkthrough: Larks are high-flying songbirds and also bits of mischief; 'Flying' points to the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Larks are pranks or bits of fun, and skylarking is playing about, so frolics fits.

clue.text: A course in confusion

blocks.note: first meaning: a dish of food
second meaning: an untidy or muddled state

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a lesson given in chaos; 'course' here is a part of a meal, an old sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess is an archaic word for a serving of food, and also a disordered or chaotic situation.

clue.text: Have a gamble in Portugal

definitions.note: a verb phrase defining a noun: the game you would play to gamble
a place found in Portugal rather than a synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: a card game played for stakes, popular in the Wild West
second meaning: the main city of the Algarve, in the south of Portugal

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a bet placed on holiday; both halves are loose, pointing at a game and a town.
explanation.definitionFit: Faro is a gambling card game in which players bet on cards drawn from a box, and also the capital of the Algarve.

clue.text: Where sailors got a suspended sentence

definitions.text: Where sailors got a suspended sentence

blocks.note: surface reading: a legal penalty that is deferred and need not be served
setter's reading: the spar from which mutinous sailors were hanged, literally suspended

explanation.walkthrough: Naval executions were carried out by hanging the man from one end of a spar on the mast.
explanation.definitionFit: A yard-arm is either end of the horizontal spar holding a square sail, the traditional gallows at sea.

clue.text: Type of relief for the handicapped

definitions.text: Type of relief for the handicapped

blocks.note: surface reading: a kind of welfare help or allowance for disabled people
setter's reading: printing type standing up in relief, raised dots read by touch by the blind

explanation.walkthrough: 'Relief' means raised printing, not aid; 'handicapped' is the dated wording of a 1970s clue for blind readers.
explanation.definitionFit: Braille is a writing system of raised dots read with the fingertips, invented by Louis Braille for blind people.

clue.text: Tear round the side and find the occupier

indicators.note: round places one piece all about the other, enclosing it

blocks.note: a rent is a tear or rip in cloth
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone rips round the side of a house and discovers who lives there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' wants to be a verb or a drop from the eye; it is the noun meaning a rip.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident is a person who lives in a place, the one occupying a house or flat.

clue.text: Christie's private eye

definitions.note: with the novelist's name as context

blocks.note: surface reading: could suggest Christie's, the London auction house, and someone watching its sales
setter's reading: the fictional Belgian detective created by Agatha Christie

explanation.walkthrough: A private eye is a detective; Agatha Christie's most famous one is a fussy Belgian with a moustache.
explanation.definitionFit: Hercule Poirot is the Belgian sleuth of Agatha Christie's novels, a private detective.
